This page goes with **Chapter 6, Triads** of Robert Hutchinson's open textbook
[*Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom*](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/Triads.html). Read each section there
first: the book is the reference for the terms and symbols used here. Then practise below. Each section has:

- a link to the book's section, and to the same topic on [musictheory.net](https://www.musictheory.net/lessons) and in
  [Open Music Theory](https://viva.pressbooks.pub/openmusictheory/chapter/triads/), for a second explanation;
- a **drill** from this site that grades every answer. You can type the answer, use the buttons, or (for naming chords) play it on a MIDI keyboard;
- musictheory.net's own exercise, folded away under the drill.

Every drill has **Settings**. Your teacher's link may set them for you; you can still change them, and **Back to the link's
settings** undoes your changes. The same drills, with all their settings, are on the [Theory Drills](theory-drills.qmd) page.

## 6.1 The four qualities

A triad is three notes stacked in thirds: the **root**, the **third** and the **fifth**. Which thirds you stack decides the
**quality**. Major and minor triads are everywhere, diminished ones less often, augmented ones rarely.
[Read 6.1](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/TriadsIntroduction.html) ·
[musictheory.net: Introduction to Chords](https://www.musictheory.net/lessons/40) ·
[Open Music Theory: Triads](https://viva.pressbooks.pub/openmusictheory/chapter/triads/)

| Quality | Root to third | Third to fifth | Root to fifth | Symbol on C |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Major | M3 (4 half steps) | m3 (3) | P5 (7) | C |
| Minor | m3 (3) | M3 (4) | P5 (7) | Cm |
| Diminished | m3 (3) | m3 (3) | d5 (6) | C° |
| Augmented | M3 (4) | M3 (4) | A5 (8) | C+ |

Start with roots that have no sharps or flats:

## 6.2 Lead-sheet symbols

A lead-sheet symbol names the root and the quality and leaves the voicing to the player: a capital letter for major (*F*), the letter
and a small *m* for minor (*Gm*), a small circle for diminished (*D°*), and a plus for augmented (*C+*). In the book's example, the
chords of Alicia Keys's "Girl on Fire" are written this way over the guitar tab.
[Read 6.2](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/LeadSheetSymbols.html) ·
[Open Music Theory: Chord Symbols](https://viva.pressbooks.pub/openmusictheory/chapter/chord-symbols/)

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

**Typing a symbol:** a capital letter is major (*A*), a small letter or a letter with *m* is minor (*a*, *Am*), *°* (or *o*) diminished, *+* augmented. Type `#` and `b` for ♯ and ♭.

## 6.3 Inverted triads and slash chords

The **root** is the bottom note when the chord is stacked in thirds; the **bass** is whatever note is actually lowest. When the third
is in the bass the triad is in **first inversion**, when the fifth is, **second inversion**. A lead-sheet symbol shows an inversion with
a slash: the chord, then the bass note. *C/E* is a C major triad with E at the bottom.
[Read 6.3](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/InvertedTriads.html) ·
[musictheory.net: Triad Inversion](https://www.musictheory.net/lessons/42) ·
[Open Music Theory: Inversion](https://viva.pressbooks.pub/openmusictheory/chapter/inversion/)

## 6.4 Naming a chord spread over the staff

In real music a triad is spread out, with notes doubled, across both staves. To name it: find the root (stack the notes in thirds), then
the quality (measure the two thirds), then the bass (is the lowest note the root?). Then write the symbol, with a slash if it is inverted.
[Read 6.4](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/AnalyzingChords.html) ·
[musictheory.net: Voicing Chords](https://www.musictheory.net/lessons/51)

<div class="drill" data-ex="triad" data-settings="quals=maj,min,dim,aug&roots=any&inv=all&voicing=spread"></div>

## 6.5 Sus chords

In a **sus4** chord a perfect 4th takes the place of the third; in a **sus2** chord a major 2nd does. Both keep the perfect 5th.
Without a third, a sus chord is neither major nor minor. The book does not invert sus chords, and neither does the drill.
[Read 6.5](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/SimpleSusChords.html) ·
[Open Music Theory: Chord Symbols, "sus"](https://viva.pressbooks.pub/openmusictheory/chapter/chord-symbols/)

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

- musictheory.net's exercises are embedded with their own default settings. A [customized exercise](https://www.musictheory.net/exercises/customize)
